solution.concept_anchor: Imperial Bank of India formation from Presidency Banks
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is deceptive because students often associate the formation of large banking institutions with the 1969 nationalization wave, conflating the Imperial Bank's 1921 origin with that later event.
elimination_logic: Eliminate (a): The Imperial Bank of India was not formed in 1935; that year marks the establishment of the Reserve Bank of India.
Eliminate (c): The Imperial Bank was not a merger of provincial banks of Calcutta, Bombay, and Lahore — it merged the three Presidency Banks.
Eliminate (d): The Bank of Hindustan is not one of the three Presidency Banks; the correct trio is Bank of Bengal, Bank of Bombay, and Bank of Madras.
Confirm (b): The Imperial Bank of India was constituted in 1921 through the merger of the Bank of Bengal, Bank of Bombay, and Bank of Madras — this is the correct statement.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap here is the entity-swap between the year 1935 (RBI's establishment) and 1921 (Imperial Bank's formation). A student who loosely recalls that 'a major banking institution was set up in the 1930s' will gravitate toward option (a). Additionally, option (d) introduces the Bank of Hindustan — a real institution from colonial times — as a plausible-sounding substitute for one of the actual Presidency Banks, catching those who cannot recall all three names precisely.
solution.final_explanation:
The Imperial Bank of India came into being in 1921 as a result of the merger of the three colonial-era Presidency Banks: the Bank of Bengal (est. 1806), the Bank of Bombay (est. 1840), and the Bank of Madras (est. 1843). It operated as the largest commercial bank in British India and also performed limited central banking functions until the Reserve Bank of India was established in 1935.

• Option (a): Incorrect. 1935 is the year of the RBI's establishment, not the Imperial Bank's formation.
• Option (b): Correct. The 1921 merger of the three Presidency Banks created the Imperial Bank.
• Option (c): Incorrect. The merged entities were the three Presidency Banks — not provincial banks of Calcutta, Bombay, and Lahore.
• Option (d): Incorrect. The Bank of Hindustan was not a Presidency Bank; it was a separate early colonial bank that failed in 1832.

Value Addition:
• The Imperial Bank was subsequently renamed the State Bank of India under the SBI Act, 1955.
• This 1955 transformation preceded the 1969 and 1980 bank nationalization waves by over a decade.
• RBI initially held the majority stake in SBI after 1955 before transferring it to the Government of India in 2007.

solution.concept_anchor: SBI statutory corporation not nationalized bank under 1955 Act

statement_analysis.statement: The State Bank of India is governed by the Banking Companies (Acquisition and Transfer of Undertakings) Act, 1970, which is the same legislation that governs most other Public Sector Banks.
statement_analysis.reason: SBI is governed by the State Bank of India Act, 1955 — a separate and earlier legislation. The 1970/1980 acquisition Acts apply to banks nationalized in those waves, not to SBI.

statement_analysis.statement: SBI is classified as a statutory corporation rather than a company incorporated under the Companies Act, which has implications for the applicability of CAG audit and RTI provisions.
statement_analysis.reason: Being constituted by a special statute (SBI Act 1955) makes SBI a statutory corporation; CAG can audit it as a government-owned entity and RTI applies given substantial government funding.

statement_analysis.statement: The Government of India assumed majority ownership of SBI from the Reserve Bank of India through an amendment to the SBI Act in 2007.
statement_analysis.reason: Under the SBI (Amendment) Act, 2007, RBI divested its majority stake in SBI to the Government of India, ending RBI's role as the majority shareholder.

solution.strong_distractor: b — A student who correctly identifies Statement 2 as true but mistakenly believes Statement 1 is also correct (confusing SBI with other PSBs) will select (b), missing that the 1970 Act does not govern SBI.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: SBI is governed by its own 1955 Act, NOT by the 1970/1980 acquisition legislation — Statement 1 is incorrect.
Evaluate Statement 2: SBI is indeed a statutory corporation, and its government ownership makes it subject to CAG audit and RTI — Statement 2 is correct.
Evaluate Statement 3: The SBI (Amendment) Act, 2007 transferred RBI's majority stake to GoI — Statement 3 is correct.
Only Statements 2 and 3 are correct, pointing to option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap in Statement 1 exploits the common conflation between SBI and other PSBs. Many students learn that 'public sector banks are governed by the 1970/1980 Acts' and apply this rule indiscriminately to SBI. In reality, SBI's pre-existing 1955 Act gives it a distinct legal standing — it was 'constituted,' not 'nationalized' in the legislative sense that applies to the 1969/1980 cohort. This distinction is highly UPSC-relevant as it affects how SBI is treated for regulatory, audit, and governance purposes.
solution.final_explanation:
The State Bank of India occupies a legally unique position among Indian banks. Unlike the banks nationalized in 1969 and 1980 — which are governed by the Banking Companies (Acquisition and Transfer of Undertakings) Act, 1970 or 1980 — SBI operates under its own special statute, the State Bank of India Act, 1955.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: SBI is not governed by the 1970 Act. That legislation applies to 14 banks nationalized in 1969. SBI's distinct 1955 Act places it outside the 'nationalized bank' category in the strict legislative sense.
• Statement 2 — Correct: As a statutory corporation, SBI is not a 'company' under the Companies Act; yet its substantial government ownership makes it subject to CAG audit and RTI applicability.
• Statement 3 — Correct: The SBI (Amendment) Act, 2007 facilitated the transfer of RBI's shareholding in SBI to the Government of India, making GoI the direct majority owner.

Value Addition:
• The State Bank of India (Subsidiary Banks) Act, 1959 is a separate legislation that governed SBI's associate banks — a frequent UPSC trap paired with the 1955 Act.
• SBI's legal status as a statutory body means its employees are not civil servants under the Constitution.
• Post-2007, both SBI and the nationalized banks ultimately have GoI as their controlling shareholder, though through different statutory routes.

solution.concept_anchor: SBI constituted not nationalized — scheduled bank privileges

statement_analysis.statement: SBI's inclusion in the Second Schedule of the RBI Act, 1934 entitles it to borrow from the RBI at the Bank Rate and makes it eligible for refinance facilities.
statement_analysis.reason: Scheduled bank status under the Second Schedule of the RBI Act carries precisely these privileges — access to RBI credit facilities and the obligation to maintain CRR.

statement_analysis.statement: In the strict legislative sense, SBI is a 'nationalized bank' because it was taken over from private ownership and placed under government control through an Act of Parliament.
statement_analysis.reason: SBI was 'constituted' as a new statutory body under the SBI Act, 1955 — it was not 'nationalized' in the manner of the 1969/1980 banks. The term 'nationalized bank' in Indian banking parlance specifically refers to banks covered by the 1970/1980 acquisition Acts.

statement_analysis.statement: As a scheduled commercial bank, SBI is required to maintain the Cash Reserve Ratio with the Reserve Bank of India.
statement_analysis.reason: Maintenance of CRR with RBI is a statutory obligation for all scheduled banks under the RBI Act and Banking Regulation Act, including SBI.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Students might eliminate Statement 3 thinking SBI has some special exemption from CRR obligations given its unique statutory status, when in fact CRR applies to SBI as it does to all scheduled banks.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: Scheduled bank status does entail borrowing privileges from RBI and refinance eligibility — Statement 1 is correct, not incorrect.
Evaluate Statement 2: SBI was 'constituted' under the 1955 Act, not 'nationalized' in the sense of the 1970/1980 Acts — Statement 2 is incorrect, making it a candidate.
Evaluate Statement 3: CRR maintenance with RBI is mandatory for all scheduled banks including SBI — Statement 3 is correct, not incorrect.
Only Statement 2 is NOT correct — option (b) is the answer.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The question exploits a widely held misconception that SBI, being a government bank established through parliamentary legislation, is a 'nationalized bank.' In Indian banking regulation, 'nationalized bank' is a term of art referring specifically to the 14 banks nationalized in 1969 and 6 banks in 1980 under the acquisition Acts. SBI's creation under a separate 1955 statute places it in a distinct legal category. A superficially prepared student will mark Statement 2 as correct, believing all government-controlled banks are 'nationalized,' and therefore miss it as the incorrect statement.
solution.final_explanation:
The distinction between SBI's 'constitution' under a special Act and the 'nationalization' of other PSBs under acquisition legislation is one of the most tested nuances in Indian banking.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Scheduled bank status under the Second Schedule of the RBI Act grants access to RBI's liquidity facilities and imposes the CRR obligation.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: SBI is NOT a 'nationalized bank' in the strict legislative sense. The Banking Companies (Acquisition and Transfer of Undertakings) Acts of 1970 and 1980 created 'nationalized banks.' SBI was 'constituted' as a statutory corporation in 1955 — a legally distinct process.
• Statement 3 — Correct: CRR maintenance with RBI is a universal obligation for all scheduled banks, including SBI.

Value Addition:
• The 14 banks nationalized in 1969 and 6 in 1980 are collectively called 'nationalized banks'; SBI and its former associates are categorised separately.
• SBI's unique statutory origin means it predates the conceptual framework of bank nationalization in India.
• This distinction matters for legal challenges: SBI employees' service conditions are governed by SBI-specific regulations, not the Banking Companies Act.

SBI vs. RBI: Distinction in Roles, Functions, and Hierarchy

solution.concept_anchor: RBI is banker to government; SBI acts as RBI's agent
solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who recall that 'SBI manages government accounts' and 'this is because RBI designated it' will select (a), failing to recognize that R describes a different legal basis than the actual causal mechanism.
elimination_logic: Step 1 — Is Assertion (A) correct? A states that SBI manages Central and State government accounts in locations where RBI has no office, acting under Section 45 of the RBI Act. This is factually accurate — A is correct.

Step 2 — Is Reason (R) correct? R states that SBI is the 'Banker to the Government' of India. This is factually incorrect — the RBI is the Banker to the Government; SBI acts as RBI's agent, not as the principal banker in its own right.
Step 3 — Since R is incorrect, the answer must be (c): A is correct but R is incorrect.
Confirm: option (c) is consistent — A is a true factual claim; R misattributes the 'Banker to the Government' designation to SBI rather than RBI.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: This is a classic hierarchy-confusion trap. Students who know that SBI handles government accounts day-to-day often mistakenly conclude that SBI itself holds the title of 'Banker to the Government.' The reality is a two-tier arrangement: the RBI Act designates RBI as the Banker to the Government, and Section 45 of the RBI Act empowers RBI to appoint SBI (and its agents) to carry out banking functions on its behalf where RBI lacks a branch. The Assertion is true; the Reason inverts the principal-agent relationship.
solution.final_explanation:
The RBI-SBI relationship in government banking involves a carefully structured principal-agent hierarchy that is frequently misunderstood.

• Assertion (A): Correct. Section 45 of the RBI Act, 1934 empowers the Reserve Bank to appoint the State Bank of India as its agent to conduct government banking business — including management of accounts and treasury operations — in locations where RBI does not maintain an office. SBI performs this function in numerous states and Union Territories.
• Reason (R): Incorrect. The designation 'Banker to the Government' belongs exclusively to the Reserve Bank of India. SBI is RBI's agent in this capacity, not an independent principal banker to the government. Conflating the two roles is the error.
• Causal relationship: Not applicable because R itself is factually wrong.

Value Addition:
• RBI's role as Banker to the Government covers both the Central Government and State Governments under different agreements.
• SBI also handles pension payments and salary disbursements for government employees as part of this agency arrangement.
• The conflict-of-interest concern arises because SBI simultaneously lends commercially and manages government accounts, creating dual incentive structures.

solution.concept_anchor: EBLR system introduction October 2019 retail MSME loans
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) is deceptive because MCLR was the immediately preceding lending rate benchmark, and students who know SBI uses MCLR but are unaware of the EBLR transition in 2019 will choose it.
elimination_logic: Eliminate (a): The Base Rate system preceded MCLR and is not the mechanism introduced in 2019 for retail and MSME loans.
Eliminate (c): MCLR (Marginal Cost of Funds based Lending Rate) was introduced in 2016 and applied broadly — EBLR specifically replaced MCLR linkage for retail and MSME segments from October 2019.
Eliminate (d): The Prime Lending Rate (PLR) is an older, pre-MCLR benchmark that was phased out; it was not introduced in 2019.
Confirm (b): The External Benchmark Lending Rate (EBLR) system, linking loan rates to external benchmarks like the RBI repo rate, was made mandatory for retail and MSME loans from October 2019.
solution.final_explanation:
Monetary policy transmission refers to the process by which changes in the RBI's policy repo rate feed through to lending rates charged by commercial banks. To improve this transmission, RBI introduced the External Benchmark Lending Rate (EBLR) system from October 1, 2019, making it mandatory for banks to link their retail (housing, auto, personal) and MSME loan rates to an external benchmark — primarily the RBI's repo rate.

• Option (a): Incorrect. The Base Rate system was introduced in 2010, replacing the benchmark prime lending rate; it predates the 2019 reform.
• Option (b): Correct. EBLR, mandatorily linked to the RBI repo rate for retail and MSME loans, was introduced in October 2019 specifically to ensure faster and more transparent transmission.
• Option (c): Incorrect. MCLR (Marginal Cost of Funds based Lending Rate) was introduced in April 2016 and applied to all new loans — EBLR subsequently replaced MCLR linkage for specific categories.
• Option (d): Incorrect. PLR (Prime Lending Rate) was the pre-2010 benchmark system, not a 2019 reform.

Value Addition:
• EBLR transmission is considered more transparent as external benchmarks (repo rate) are publicly observable and reset at least every three months.
• The 'stickiness' problem under MCLR arose because banks could delay passing rate cuts to borrowers.
• SBI's size means its EBLR-linked rate decisions signal expected rate trends for the entire banking system.

SBI's Capital Adequacy and Basel Norms Compliance

solution.concept_anchor: D-SIB framework SBI Bucket 4 G-SIB distinction

statement_analysis.statement: RBI's framework for identifying Domestic Systemically Important Banks (D-SIBs) considers parameters such as size, interconnectedness, substitutability, and complexity of the bank.
statement_analysis.reason: The RBI's D-SIB methodology (2014) explicitly uses these four parameters to assess systemic importance and assign banks to buckets.

statement_analysis.statement: SBI has been placed in the highest bucket under the D-SIB framework, requiring it to maintain an additional Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) capital surcharge of 0.60% of Risk Weighted Assets.
statement_analysis.reason: SBI is in Bucket 4 — the highest bucket — and is accordingly required to hold an additional CET1 surcharge of 0.60%, the highest among D-SIBs in India.

statement_analysis.statement: Since SBI has been designated as a D-SIB by RBI, it has also been included in the Financial Stability Board's list of Global Systemically Important Banks (G-SIBs).
statement_analysis.reason: D-SIB designation by RBI and G-SIB designation by the FSB are separate frameworks with different criteria; SBI is NOT on the FSB's G-SIB list.

solution.strong_distractor: d — A student who is confident about Statements 1 and 2 but incorrectly assumes that D-SIB status automatically confers G-SIB recognition will select (d), unaware that these are distinct frameworks with independent criteria.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: Size, interconnectedness, substitutability, and complexity are the four D-SIB assessment parameters per RBI's 2014 framework — Statement 1 is correct.
Evaluate Statement 2: SBI is in Bucket 4, the highest, with a 0.60% additional CET1 surcharge — Statement 2 is correct.
Evaluate Statement 3: D-SIB and G-SIB are distinct designations by different authorities (RBI vs. FSB); SBI is not on the G-SIB list — Statement 3 is incorrect.
Only Statements 1 and 2 are correct — option (a).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap in Statement 3 exploits conflation between the domestic (D-SIB) and global (G-SIB) systemic importance frameworks. Students who know SBI is India's largest bank and is designated as the most systemically important domestic bank naturally assume this translates into global designation. The FSB's G-SIB list (which includes banks like JPMorgan, HSBC, and ICBC) is determined by global size and cross-border activity metrics, and SBI's global footprint does not meet those thresholds. This is a classic UPSC trap pairing a correct domestic fact with a falsely extrapolated global implication.
solution.final_explanation:
The D-SIB framework was introduced by RBI in 2014 to identify banks whose failure could pose systemic risks to the Indian financial system. Banks are assessed on four dimensions — size, interconnectedness, substitutability, and complexity — and placed in buckets with corresponding additional capital requirements.

• Statement 1 — Correct: RBI's D-SIB assessment methodology explicitly uses these four parameters. Higher scores lead to higher bucket placement.
• Statement 2 — Correct: SBI is placed in Bucket 4 — the highest category among Indian D-SIBs — requiring an additional CET1 surcharge of 0.60% of Risk-Weighted Assets. ICICI Bank and HDFC Bank are in lower buckets.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: D-SIB designation is a purely domestic classification by RBI. The Financial Stability Board (FSB) independently determines the G-SIB list based on global systemic importance metrics. SBI is not included in the FSB's G-SIB list.

Value Addition:
• The three Indian D-SIBs are SBI (Bucket 4), HDFC Bank, and ICICI Bank.
• D-SIB surcharge must be maintained in the form of Common Equity Tier 1 capital only — Tier 2 capital does not qualify.
• India's minimum CRAR requirement is 9%, higher than the Basel III minimum of 8%, reflecting RBI's conservative approach.

solution.concept_anchor: SBI Act 1955 vs Subsidiary Banks Act 1959 legislative distinction
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) incorrectly pairs the SBI (Subsidiary Banks) Act, 1959 with governing SBI's core operations. Students who conflate the two SBI-related Acts will be attracted to this option.
elimination_logic: Match A (SBI Act, 1955): This Act constituted SBI itself and governs its core operations — matches with 3.
Match B (SBI Subsidiary Banks Act, 1959): This Act governed the associate/subsidiary banks of SBI — matches with 1.
Match C (Banking Regulation Act, 1949): This is the primary regulatory legislation for banks broadly, under which RBI exercises supervisory powers — matches with 4.
Match D (RBI Act, 1934, Section 45): This section empowers RBI to appoint SBI as its agent for government banking — matches with 2. Correct combination: A-3, B-1, C-4, D-2 → option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The primary trap is between List I items A and B — both are SBI-related statutes, and students often swap their scope. The SBI Act, 1955 created SBI itself; the SBI (Subsidiary Banks) Act, 1959 created the framework for SBI's associate banks. An additional trap is matching Section 45 of the RBI Act with government account management — students who recall that SBI manages government accounts may attribute this to the SBI Act rather than the RBI Act provision that actually authorizes it.
solution.final_explanation:
This question tests the ability to distinguish between closely related banking statutes and their specific functions.

• A – SBI Act, 1955 → 3 (Constituted SBI as a statutory corporation and governs its core structure): The 1955 Act is the foundational charter for SBI itself.
• B – SBI (Subsidiary Banks) Act, 1959 → 1 (Provided the framework for SBI's associate banks): This distinct legislation governed entities like State Bank of Mysore and State Bank of Patiala — not SBI's own operations.
• C – Banking Regulation Act, 1949 → 4 (Primary legislation under which RBI exercises supervisory and regulatory powers over banks): This is the overarching banking regulation statute, though SBI has some exemptions.
• D – Section 45 of RBI Act, 1934 → 2 (Empowers RBI to appoint SBI as its agent for government banking in places where RBI has no office): This is the precise provision that creates the SBI-as-agent arrangement.

Correct match: A-3, B-1, C-4, D-2 → option (c).

Value Addition:
• The SBI (Subsidiary Banks) Act, 1959 became largely redundant after the 2017 merger of all associate banks.
• Banking Regulation Act, 1949 applies to SBI alongside the SBI Act — creating a dual regulatory framework.
• After the 2007 amendment, GoI replaced RBI as majority shareholder of SBI under the SBI Act itself.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Students who know NABARD is involved in rural credit planning may attribute the lead coordination role to NABARD, not recognizing that the Lead Bank Scheme places a commercial bank (not NABARD) in the district-level coordination role.
elimination_logic: The scenario describes district-level credit coordination, convening of local banker committees, and preparation of annual credit plans — these are hallmarks of the Lead Bank Scheme.
Eliminate (a): The Priority Sector Lending mandate requires banks to lend specific percentages to target sectors but does not involve district-level coordination committees or ACP preparation.
Eliminate (c): NABARD refinances cooperative banks and RRBs at the state level; it does not serve as the lead coordinator at the district level in the manner described.
Eliminate (d): Business Correspondent deployment is a last-mile service delivery mechanism, not a coordination framework involving multiple banks and government departments.
Confirm (b): The Lead Bank Scheme assigns one bank per district to coordinate credit planning, convene DCCs, and prepare Annual Credit Plans — matching all elements of the scenario.
solution.final_explanation:
The Lead Bank Scheme, introduced in 1969 on the recommendations of the Gadgil Study Group and Narasimham Working Group, assigns one commercial bank (the 'lead bank') to each district. The lead bank coordinates credit planning, convenes District Consultative Committees (DCCs), prepares Annual Credit Plans (ACPs), and liaises with district administration and other financial institutions.

• Option (a) — Priority Sector Lending mandate: Incorrect. PSL specifies percentage targets for lending to agriculture, MSMEs, and weaker sections but does not create a district-level coordination architecture.
• Option (b) — Lead Bank Scheme: Correct. The scenario precisely describes the lead bank's role — district coordination, DCC convening, ACP preparation, and liaison between multiple lenders and the government.
• Option (c) — NABARD's refinancing mandate: Incorrect. NABARD operates at the state level, refinancing cooperative banks and RRBs. It does not function as the district-level credit coordinator.
• Option (d) — Business Correspondent model: Incorrect. BC deployment extends banking services to underserved areas through agents but does not involve the inter-institutional coordination described.

Value Addition:
• State Level Bankers' Committee (SLBC) is the state-level equivalent; SBI is convener in several states.
• Each district can have only one lead bank; large banks like SBI lead a significant number of districts.
• SLBC conveners are typically the largest public sector bank operating in that state.

solution.strong_distractor: b — The UPSC Appointments Committee of the Cabinet sounds administratively authoritative, and students unfamiliar with the specific SBI appointment process may believe this body plays a role in SBI Chairman's appointment, as it does for many senior government positions.
elimination_logic: Identify what the question asks: which body does NOT have a formal role in the SBI appointment/governance ecosystem as described in the SBI Act and related frameworks.
Government of India: Directly appoints the SBI Chairman in consultation with RBI — has a clear role.
Reserve Bank of India: Consulted during appointment of SBI Chairman — has a clear role.
Financial Services Institutions Bureau (FSIB): Recommends candidates for appointment to SBI's top positions — has a clear role.

Appointments Committee of the Cabinet: While this body approves many government appointments, SBI-specific appointments follow the SBI Act framework through FSIB recommendations to the Finance Ministry — not through ACC in the same manner. The odd one out is (d).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The Appointments Committee of the Cabinet (ACC) is a real and powerful government body that approves appointments to senior positions across many departments and public sector undertakings. However, appointments to SBI's Chairman and Managing Director positions follow a specific route under the SBI Act — recommendations from FSIB (formerly Banks Board Bureau) go to the Government of India (Finance Ministry), which makes the appointment in consultation with RBI. The ACC's direct role in SBI appointments is not established in the same way, making it the institutional odd-one-out in this specific governance context.
solution.final_explanation:
SBI's governance appointments are governed by the SBI Act, 1955 and related frameworks that involve specific institutions.

• Option (a) — Government of India: Has a direct role; the GoI appoints the SBI Chairman in consultation with RBI under the SBI Act.
• Option (b) — Reserve Bank of India: Has a formal consultative role in the appointment of SBI's Chairman and is SBI's primary regulator.
• Option (c) — Financial Services Institutions Bureau (FSIB): Replaced the Banks Board Bureau (BBB) and recommends candidates for top positions in PSBs and financial institutions including SBI.
• Option (d) — Appointments Committee of the Cabinet: While it approves many government appointments, SBI's Chairman appointment specifically follows the SBI Act route (FSIB → Finance Ministry → GoI in consultation with RBI) rather than the standard ACC route.

Value Addition:
• The Banks Board Bureau (BBB) was renamed the Financial Services Institutions Bureau (FSIB) following a Delhi High Court ruling on its scope.
• SBI's Chairman is appointed for a fixed term; the Managing Directors are also appointed through FSIB recommendations.
• Unlike RBI's Governor (appointed purely by GoI), SBI's Chairman appointment mandates RBI consultation — reflecting SBI's hybrid commercial-public character.

solution.concept_anchor: RBI majority shareholder SBI until 2007 ownership transition

statement_analysis.statement: Statement 1: The Reserve Bank of India was the majority shareholder of the State Bank of India from SBI's constitution in 1955 until it divested this stake to the Government of India in 2007.
statement_analysis.reason: Under the SBI Act, 1955, RBI initially held the majority stake. The SBI (Amendment) Act, 2007 facilitated the transfer of this stake to the Government of India, making GoI the direct majority shareholder.

statement_analysis.statement: Statement 2: Since the RBI is the majority owner of SBI, it also serves as the consolidated supervisor of the SBI group, overseeing its insurance and asset management subsidiaries through the FSDC framework.
statement_analysis.reason: RBI is no longer the majority owner of SBI — it divested in 2007. Furthermore, RBI's role as consolidated supervisor of the SBI group stems from its regulatory mandate, not from ownership. The statement is doubly incorrect.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Students may recall that RBI supervises SBI and also that RBI has some connection to SBI's ownership history, and conclude both statements are broadly true without catching the 2007 divestment detail.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: RBI held majority stake from 1955; the 2007 amendment transferred it to GoI — Statement 1 is correct.
Evaluate Statement 2: The premise 'RBI is the majority owner of SBI' is factually wrong as of 2007; GoI is the majority owner. The statement is incorrect.
Since Statement 1 is correct and Statement 2 is incorrect, the answer is option (c).
Confirm: option (c) states 'Statement 1 is correct but Statement 2 is incorrect' — this matches our analysis.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap is a temporal error. Students who know that 'RBI was SBI's majority shareholder' without registering that this ended in 2007 will treat Statement 2's ownership premise as true. The question exploits the common habit of treating historical facts as current facts — a frequent UPSC trap mechanism in banking questions.
solution.final_explanation:
The ownership structure of SBI has undergone a significant transition that is often tested.

• Statement 1 — Correct: When SBI was constituted under the SBI Act, 1955, RBI was designated as its principal shareholder holding the majority stake. This arrangement persisted until the SBI (Amendment) Act, 2007, which enabled RBI to transfer its shareholding to the Government of India. Post-2007, GoI directly holds the majority stake in SBI.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: This statement contains two errors. First, RBI is no longer SBI's majority owner — that transfer occurred in 2007. Second, RBI's role as consolidated supervisor for the SBI group (covering its insurance and mutual fund subsidiaries) arises from its regulatory mandate under the Financial Stability and Development Council (FSDC) inter-regulatory framework, not from ownership.

Value Addition:
• Even after divesting its stake, RBI retains its regulatory and supervisory role over SBI — ownership and regulation are legally separate.
• The 2007 transfer also had fiscal implications: GoI's balance sheet now directly carries the SBI investment.
• RBI's role as consolidated supervisor ensures that risks from SBI's subsidiaries (SBI Life, SBI MF) are monitored at the group level.

solution.concept_anchor: SBI as Primary Dealer in Government Securities market
solution.strong_distractor: b — 'Authorised Dealer' is a real designation under FEMA for foreign exchange transactions, and SBI does hold this status; students who recall this designation may incorrectly apply it to the G-Sec market context.
elimination_logic: The question describes underwiting and market-making in Government Securities — this is the exclusive function of Primary Dealers.
Eliminate (b): 'Authorised Dealer' is a FEMA designation for foreign exchange, not for G-Sec market participation.
Eliminate (c): 'Market Maker of Last Resort' is not a formal designation in Indian financial markets.
Eliminate (d): 'Scheduled Commercial Bank' describes SBI's general category but does not specifically authorize G-Sec underwriting and market-making.
Confirm (a): Primary Dealer (PD) status is the specific designation that confers the obligation and privilege to underwrite government securities and maintain two-way quotes in the G-Sec market.
solution.final_explanation:
In India's government securities market, the Reserve Bank of India relies on a network of Primary Dealers (PDs) to ensure market liquidity and successful government borrowing. PDs are obligated to submit bids at primary auctions and maintain two-way quotes in the secondary market.

• Option (a) — Primary Dealer: Correct. SBI holds PD status, enabling it to underwrite Government Securities (G-Secs), State Development Loans (SDLs), and Treasury Bills, and to make secondary markets.
• Option (b) — Authorised Dealer (Category I): Incorrect. This designation applies under FEMA for foreign exchange transactions, not for G-Sec market operations.
• Option (c) — Market Maker of Last Resort: Incorrect. This is not a formal designation in the RBI framework; 'lender of last resort' is RBI's role, not a market designation for SBI.
• Option (d) — Scheduled Commercial Bank: Incorrect. While SBI is a scheduled commercial bank, this general classification does not confer the specific G-Sec underwriting obligation.

Value Addition:
• There are two categories of PDs: Standalone PDs (non-bank entities) and Bank PDs (like SBI).
• When the proposed Public Debt Management Agency (PDMA) is established, it may alter the current PD framework.
• SBI also participates in the Sovereign Gold Bond (SGB) scheme as a receiving office for public subscriptions.

solution.concept_anchor: AQR 2015 IBC 2016 sequence NPA resolution timeline
solution.strong_distractor: c — Students who remember that 'IBC came before the AQR' — perhaps confusing the IBC's legislative passage date (May 2016) with the AQR which was announced in late 2015 — may select option (c), inverting the actual sequence.
elimination_logic: SARFAESI Act: Enacted in 2002 — clearly the earliest of the three events.
Asset Quality Review (AQR): Initiated by RBI in late 2015 to compel banks to recognize hidden NPAs — second in sequence.
Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC): Enacted in May 2016 — after the AQR exposed the NPA scale, creating urgency for a resolution mechanism.
Correct sequence: SARFAESI (2002) → AQR (2015) → IBC (2016) — option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The key trap is the AQR-IBC ordering. Both occurred close together (late 2015 and mid-2016), and students may confuse which preceded which. The AQR was the RBI's diagnostic tool that revealed the true scale of bank NPAs; this recognition of the problem then created regulatory pressure to enact a stronger resolution mechanism, which materialized as the IBC in 2016. Students who think of IBC as a 'bigger' reform sometimes erroneously place it before the AQR.
solution.final_explanation:
Understanding the timeline of NPA recognition and resolution mechanisms is essential for comprehending India's banking sector reforms.

Correct sequence: SARFAESI Act (2002) → Asset Quality Review (2015) → Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (2016) — option (b).

• SARFAESI Act, 2002: The Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interests Act was India's first major secured creditor enforcement legislation, giving banks the power to recover dues without court intervention in many cases.
• Asset Quality Review (AQR), 2015: RBI's RBI's directed inspection of bank loan books to ensure consistent NPA classification. It led to a sharp jump in reported NPAs as hidden stressed assets were recognized, dramatically increasing SBI's disclosed NPA levels.
• Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC), 2016: Enacted in May 2016 as a comprehensive time-bound resolution framework, consolidating over a dozen earlier laws. It created the NCLT-based resolution process that SBI uses as the largest institutional creditor in many large NPA cases.

Value Addition:
• Debt Recovery Tribunals (DRTs) predate SARFAESI — established under the Recovery of Debts Due to Banks Act, 1993.
• SBI's Stressed Assets Management Group (SAMG) is its internal body for coordinating large NPA resolutions.
• Under IBC, SBI frequently leads Joint Lenders' Forums as the bank with the highest exposure in large infrastructure defaults.

solution.concept_anchor: Priority Sector Lending 40% ANBC target sub-targets agriculture
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) places the agriculture sub-target at 20% of ANBC, which sounds plausible to students who know the overall PSL target is 40% and may guess that agriculture gets 'about half of that.' The actual target is 18%.
elimination_logic: Eliminate (a): 'Priority Sector Lending requires 50% of ANBC for SBI' — the actual overall PSL target is 40% of Adjusted Net Bank Credit, not 50%.
Eliminate (b): 'Agriculture sub-target under PSL is 20% of ANBC' — the actual agriculture sub-target is 18% of ANBC, not 20%.
Eliminate (c): 'Small and Marginal Farmers sub-target is 12% of ANBC' — the actual sub-target for small and marginal farmers is 8% of ANBC.
Confirm (d): 'Overall PSL target is 40% of ANBC' — this is correct; the aggregate Priority Sector Lending target for scheduled commercial banks including SBI is 40% of Adjusted Net Bank Credit.
solution.final_explanation:
Priority Sector Lending (PSL) mandates require banks to direct a specified portion of their credit to designated priority sectors including agriculture, MSMEs, export credit, education, housing, social infrastructure, and renewable energy.

• Option (a) — '50% of ANBC for SBI': Incorrect. The overall PSL target is 40% of Adjusted Net Bank Credit for all scheduled commercial banks, including SBI. There is no 50% figure.
• Option (b) — 'Agriculture sub-target is 20% of ANBC': Incorrect. The agriculture sub-target under PSL is 18% of ANBC. A further sub-target of 8% exists for credit to small and marginal farmers within this 18%.
• Option (c) — 'Small and marginal farmers sub-target is 12%': Incorrect. This sub-target is 8% of ANBC, not 12%.
• Option (d) — 'Overall PSL target is 40% of ANBC': Correct. This is the mandated aggregate target applicable to domestic scheduled commercial banks.

Value Addition:
• Banks failing to meet PSL targets must deposit the shortfall amount into the Rural Infrastructure Development Fund (RIDF) maintained with NABARD.
• Foreign banks with fewer than 20 branches have a lower PSL target of 40% but with different sector compositions.
• ANBC is computed as Net Bank Credit plus investments in non-SLR bonds in HTM category.

solution.concept_anchor: NPCI ownership YONO SBI Cards separation digital ecosystem

statement_analysis.statement: YONO (You Only Need One) is SBI's integrated digital banking and lifestyle platform that serves as the bank's primary response to competition from fintech companies and digital payment aggregators.
statement_analysis.reason: YONO was launched by SBI as an integrated platform combining banking services with lifestyle features (shopping, travel, insurance), explicitly positioned as SBI's fintech response.

statement_analysis.statement: The National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI) is jointly owned by the Reserve Bank of India and the State Bank of India, with SBI being the largest single shareholder.
statement_analysis.reason: NPCI is an umbrella institution promoted by RBI and the Indian Banks' Association (IBA), with shareholding distributed among member banks. SBI is a member but not the largest shareholder, and NPCI is not 'owned' by RBI and SBI jointly.

statement_analysis.statement: SBI Cards and Payment Services Limited, which operates SBI's credit card business, is a listed subsidiary of SBI and is therefore subject to SEBI's regulations as a listed company, separate from RBI's direct oversight of core banking.
statement_analysis.reason: SBI Card was separately listed on stock exchanges and, as a listed entity engaged in credit card business, is subject to SEBI's listing regulations while its financial products are overseen by RBI; it operates distinctly from SBI's core banking entity.

solution.strong_distractor: d — A student who vaguely recalls that NPCI has government connections and SBI is a large bank might select (d) assuming all three statements are correct, without catching the specific error about NPCI's ownership structure.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: YONO is indeed SBI's integrated digital banking and lifestyle platform — Statement 1 is correct.
Evaluate Statement 2: NPCI is promoted by RBI and IBA (Indian Banks' Association), not jointly owned by RBI and SBI. SBI is one of many member banks — Statement 2 is incorrect.
Evaluate Statement 3: SBI Card is a separately listed subsidiary subject to SEBI listing regulations, while its credit operations are overseen by RBI — Statement 3 is correct.
Statements 1 and 3 are correct — option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2's error exploits a common conflation between NPCI's promoter banks and its actual ownership structure. Students know that RBI plays a central role in India's payments infrastructure and that SBI is the largest bank, and they assume NPCI is a joint venture between these two dominant entities. In reality, NPCI was incorporated as a Section 8 company (not-for-profit) under the Companies Act, with shareholding broadly distributed among member banks under RBI and IBA's promotion — no single bank dominates its ownership.
solution.final_explanation:
SBI's digital ecosystem and India's payments infrastructure involve several distinct institutional arrangements.

• Statement 1 — Correct: YONO (You Only Need One) is SBI's super-app combining banking, investment, insurance, shopping, and travel services. It was launched in 2017 as SBI's strategic response to fintech disruption.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: NPCI was promoted by RBI and the Indian Banks' Association (IBA) and is structured as a Section 8 company (not-for-profit). Its shareholding includes multiple scheduled commercial banks — not just RBI and SBI. Calling it a joint SBI-RBI entity misrepresents its structure.
• Statement 3 — Correct: SBI Cards and Payment Services (SBI Card) was listed on BSE and NSE in March 2020. As a listed entity, it is subject to SEBI's disclosure and listing obligations, while its non-banking financial activities are regulated by RBI.

Value Addition:
• NPCI operates key systems including UPI, IMPS, NACH, RuPay, and FASTag.
• SBI's share of UPI transactions has declined as private sector bank apps (PhonePe, Google Pay) dominate volumes.
• SBI holds approximately 69% stake in SBI Card; Carlyle Group holds a minority stake.

solution.concept_anchor: Lead Bank Scheme 1969 Gadgil Study Group Narasimham Working Group
solution.strong_distractor: b — The Narasimham Committee is strongly associated with banking sector reforms in 1991 and 1998. Students who recall that Narasimham was involved in banking may assume the Lead Bank Scheme originated from those reports, confusing the 1969 Narasimham Working Group with the 1991/1998 Narasimham Committees.
elimination_logic: Eliminate (b): The 1991 Narasimham Committee on Financial System and 1998 Narasimham Committee on Banking Reforms are different bodies from the 1969 Narasimham Working Group; the Lead Bank Scheme predates the 1991 reforms.
Eliminate (c): The Rangarajan Committee is associated with poverty estimation and financial inclusion in different contexts, not the Lead Bank Scheme's origin.
Eliminate (d): The Chakravarty Committee (1985) dealt with the working of the monetary system, not the district-level lead bank framework.
Confirm (a): The Lead Bank Scheme (1969) was recommended by the Gadgil Study Group and the Narasimham Working Group — both operating in 1969, distinct from later committees.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The Narasimham entity-swap is the central trap. Three significant banking committees carried the Narasimham name: the 1969 Working Group (Lead Bank Scheme), the 1991 Committee on the Financial System, and the 1998 Committee on Banking Sector Reforms. UPSC frequently tests whether students can distinguish between these different Narasimham bodies. A student who hears 'Narasimham' and banking will instinctively think of 1991/1998 liberalization reforms, missing that a different Narasimham Working Group in 1969 recommended the Lead Bank Scheme.
solution.final_explanation:
The Lead Bank Scheme is one of the foundational mechanisms for coordinating district-level credit delivery in India.

• Option (a): Correct. The Lead Bank Scheme was introduced in 1969 based on recommendations of both the Gadgil Study Group (which examined deposit mobilization in rural areas) and the Narasimham Working Group (1969) — a different body from the later Narasimham Committees of 1991 and 1998.
• Option (b): Incorrect. The Narasimham Committees of 1991 and 1998 dealt with financial system reforms and banking sector efficiency, not the Lead Bank Scheme.
• Option (c): Incorrect. Rangarajan Committee recommendations relate to poverty estimation methodology and financial inclusion, not the Lead Bank Scheme.
• Option (d): Incorrect. The Chakravarty Committee (1985) examined the working of the monetary system in India — unrelated to Lead Bank Scheme origins.

Value Addition:
• The Lead Bank Scheme coincided with the bank nationalization wave of 1969, reflecting the government's intent to use banks as development tools.
• Under the scheme, each district is assigned one bank; SBI leads numerous districts, particularly in states where it is the dominant bank.
• District Consultative Committees (DCCs) and State Level Bankers' Committees (SLBCs) are the institutional architecture created under this scheme.

solution.concept_anchor: SBI vs NABARD distinct roles RRB sponsorship ownership pattern

statement_analysis.statement: NABARD refinances scheduled commercial banks like SBI for their direct agricultural lending, just as it refinances Regional Rural Banks and cooperative banks.
statement_analysis.reason: NABARD provides refinance primarily to State Cooperative Banks, District Central Cooperative Banks, Regional Rural Banks, and State Governments — not directly to scheduled commercial banks like SBI for their regular agricultural lending. SBI lends directly from its own resources.

statement_analysis.statement: In Regional Rural Banks sponsored by SBI, the Government of India holds the largest single share of 50%, while SBI holds 35% and the concerned State Government holds 15%.
statement_analysis.reason: The RRB ownership pattern is precisely GoI 50%, Sponsor Bank 35%, State Government 15% — making GoI the dominant shareholder.

statement_analysis.statement: SBI is the largest issuer of Kisan Credit Cards among all scheduled commercial banks in India.
statement_analysis.reason: Given SBI's dominant market share in agricultural credit and its extensive rural branch network, SBI is consistently the largest KCC issuer among scheduled commercial banks.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Students who broadly know that NABARD supports the agricultural credit system may assume it refinances all types of agricultural lenders, including SBI, without distinguishing the specific channel through which NABARD operates.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: NABARD's refinance window is not extended to scheduled commercial banks for their direct farm credit — Statement 1 is incorrect (NOT correct).
Evaluate Statement 2: The 50% (GoI) – 35% (Sponsor Bank) – 15% (State) structure is accurately stated — Statement 2 is correct.
Evaluate Statement 3: SBI's dominant position in agricultural lending makes it the largest KCC issuer — Statement 3 is correct.
Only Statement 1 is NOT correct — option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 1 exploits a scope-extension error: students know NABARD supports agricultural credit and refinances rural lenders, and they extend this — incorrectly — to include SBI's direct lending. In reality, NABARD's refinance channel is specifically designed for cooperative credit institutions and RRBs, which lack the capital market access that scheduled commercial banks like SBI enjoy. SBI borrows from the capital markets, accepts deposits, and lends from its own balance sheet without relying on NABARD's refinance for its direct agricultural portfolio.
solution.final_explanation:
The SBI-NABARD distinction in agricultural credit is a high-frequency UPSC testing area.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: NABARD's refinance operations primarily target State Cooperative Banks, District Central Cooperative Banks, Regional Rural Banks, and State Governments. SBI, as a large scheduled commercial bank with direct access to capital markets and deposit mobilization, does not rely on NABARD refinance for its direct agricultural lending. The two operate in parallel but distinct channels.
• Statement 2 — Correct: RRB ownership follows a fixed pattern — GoI: 50%, Sponsor Bank: 35%, State Government: 15%. For SBI-sponsored RRBs like Kaveri Grameena Bank, SBI holds 35%.
• Statement 3 — Correct: SBI's extensive rural branch network and large agricultural credit portfolio make it the largest Kisan Credit Card issuer among scheduled commercial banks.

Value Addition:
• NABARD was established in 1982 under the NABARD Act, 1981 to serve as the apex institution for agricultural and rural credit.
• Kisan Credit Cards provide farmers with revolving credit for crop production, post-harvest expenses, and allied activities.
• India has over 40 RRBs post-amalgamation; SBI sponsors a few of these in specific states.

statement_analysis.reason: RBI is designated as the consolidated supervisor for bank-led financial conglomerates like the SBI group; inter-regulatory coordination happens through the FSDC (Financial Stability and Development Council).

solution.strong_distractor: d — A student who correctly identifies the first three statements and doesn't scrutinize Statement 4 carefully will select 'All four' without catching the IRDAI-versus-SEBI regulatory swap for SBI Capital Markets.

Evaluate Statement 2: SBI MF — mutual fund → SEBI as regulator. Correct.
Evaluate Statement 3: RBI as consolidated supervisor of bank-led conglomerates under FSDC framework. Correct.
Evaluate Statement 4: SBI Capital Markets is an investment banking entity regulated by SEBI, not IRDAI — Statement 4 is incorrect.

solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 4 deploys a regulatory entity-swap: replacing SEBI (the correct regulator for investment banking and merchant banking) with IRDAI (the insurance regulator). Students who rush through and see 'SBI subsidiary + regulatory body' may not pause to verify whether an investment banking arm could plausibly be regulated by an insurance authority. The answer 'All four' is designed to attract students who correctly verify the first three and assume the fourth must also be correct.
solution.final_explanation:
The SBI group operates as a financial conglomerate with subsidiaries regulated by three different sector regulators.

• SBI Life Insurance → Correct: Regulated by IRDAI for its life insurance products, distribution, and solvency requirements. SBI holds approximately 55% stake.
• SBI Mutual Fund (SBI Funds Management) → Correct: Regulated by SEBI under mutual fund regulations. It is India's largest AMC by AUM.
• RBI as consolidated supervisor → Correct: RBI serves as the consolidated supervisor for the SBI group to assess group-level risks, with inter-regulatory coordination through FSDC where SEBI and IRDAI also participate.
• SBI Capital Markets → Incorrect: As an investment bank and merchant banker handling IPOs and PSU disinvestment, it is regulated by SEBI — not IRDAI. IRDAI's jurisdiction is limited to insurance entities.

Three of four pairs are correct → option (c).

• Consolidated supervision ensures that risks taken by SBI's non-banking subsidiaries are factored into the group's overall risk assessment.
• SBI Card (credit card subsidiary) is regulated by RBI as an NBFC, distinct from SBI's core banking entity.

solution.concept_anchor: Bank consolidation D-SIB capital surcharge implications of scale
solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who confirm both facts and intuitively assume that 'bigger bank → more systemic risk → higher capital requirement' constitutes a causal explanation will select (a), not recognizing that the D-SIB surcharge is independently triggered by the D-SIB framework's own bucket assignment methodology, not directly by the consolidation event itself.
elimination_logic: Step 1 — Is Assertion (A) correct? A states that post-2017 merger SBI became India's largest bank with a balance sheet exceeding ₹20 lakh crore and ranked among the top 50 globally. This is factually accurate — A is correct.

Step 2 — Is Reason (R) correct? R states that Narasimham Committee (1991) recommended a 3-tier structure with 3 large international banks, 8-10 national banks, and local banks. This is factually accurate — R is correct.

Step 3 — Does R causally explain A? R describes a committee recommendation from 1991; A describes the outcome of the 2017 merger. While conceptually related (consolidation theme), the 1991 recommendation did not directly cause or explain the specific 2017 merger outcome described in A. The causal link is absent.

Both A and R are correct, but R does not causally explain A — option (b)... Wait: re-reading the options, option (b) is 'Both A and R are correct, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.' This matches. Correct option is (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap is a causal disconnection between two true facts. Students who confirm that A (SBI's post-merger scale) and R (Narasimham's 1991 consolidation recommendation) are both true will default to option (a) — 'both correct, R explains A.' However, a committee recommendation from 1991 cannot serve as the direct causal explanation for a specific 2017 governmental decision; the merger had multiple immediate drivers including RBI's Basel III capital requirements, the government's recapitalization burden, and competitive pressures — not merely a 26-year-old committee report. R and A are thematically connected but not causally linked.
solution.final_explanation:
Bank consolidation in India and its relationship to committee recommendations is a nuanced topic.

• Assertion (A): Correct. The April 2017 merger of five associate banks and Bharatiya Mahila Bank with SBI created India's largest bank with a consolidated balance sheet exceeding ₹20 lakh crore, placing SBI among the top 50 global banks by asset size.
• Reason (R): Correct. The Narasimham Committee on the Financial System (1991) explicitly recommended restructuring Indian banking into a 3-tier hierarchy: 3 large banks with international presence, 8-10 national banks, and a set of local/regional banks. The 1998 Narasimham Committee reiterated similar consolidation themes.
• Causal relationship: R does NOT causally explain A. While the Narasimham recommendation provided an intellectual framework for consolidation, the immediate drivers of the 2017 merger were operational (reducing inter-PSB competition), regulatory (Basel III capital requirements), and fiscal (reducing the government's recapitalization burden). The 1991 recommendation is thematically relevant but not the direct cause of the 2017 outcome.

Correct option: (b) — Both A and R are correct, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.

Value Addition:
• The 2019-20 PSB merger wave (under which 10 banks were merged into 4) reduced the total number of PSBs from 27 to 12.
• Consolidation critics warn of increased concentration risk and D-SIB capital surcharge implications for merged entities.
• Narasimham Committee's recommended 3-tier banking structure was never formally adopted as policy but influenced all subsequent consolidation discussions.

solution.concept_anchor: SBI Authorised Dealer Category I FEMA foreign exchange
solution.strong_distractor: c — 'Foreign Exchange Management Agent (Class A)' sounds like a plausible official designation for a bank with extensive forex operations, and students unfamiliar with FEMA's specific terminology may choose it over the actual 'Authorised Dealer Category I' designation.
elimination_logic: Eliminate (a): 'Designated Foreign Currency Institution (DFCI)' is not a formal FEMA designation; it is a fabricated term.
Eliminate (c): 'Foreign Exchange Management Agent (Class A)' is not a FEMA designation — this is a plausible-fabrication distractor.

Eliminate (d): 'Category II Authorised Money Changer' is a real but lower-tier FEMA designation for restricted forex operations (like money changers) — not applicable to a full-service international bank like SBI.
Confirm (b): Under FEMA, banks authorized to deal in all foreign exchange transactions are designated as 'Authorised Dealers Category I' — the appropriate designation for SBI.
solution.final_explanation:
Under the Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999, entities authorized to deal in foreign exchange transactions are classified based on the scope of operations they are permitted to conduct.

• Option (a) — Designated Foreign Currency Institution (DFCI): Incorrect. This is not a formal FEMA designation; the term does not exist in FEMA's regulatory framework.
• Option (b) — Authorised Dealer Category I: Correct. AD Category I is the highest tier of forex authorization under FEMA, allowing the holder to conduct the full range of foreign exchange transactions including trade finance, external commercial borrowings, capital account transactions, and remittances. SBI holds this designation.
• Option (c) — Foreign Exchange Management Agent (Class A): Incorrect. This is a fabricated designation not found in FEMA's framework.
• Option (d) — Category II Authorised Money Changer: Incorrect. Money changers and small forex bureaus may hold AD Category II or Full Fledged Money Changer status — these are limited licenses inappropriate for a full-service commercial bank like SBI.

Value Addition:
• AD Category I banks can also participate in NOSTRO and VOSTRO account management for international trade settlements.
• SBI's overseas network supports India's trade finance and remittance flows, including rupee trade with certain countries.
• RBI issues AD Category I licenses; SEBI separately licenses stock brokers and portfolio managers for capital market transactions.

solution.concept_anchor: India CRAR 9% vs Basel III 8% D-SIB surcharge CET1

statement_analysis.statement: Statement 1: India's minimum Capital to Risk-weighted Assets Ratio (CRAR) requirement for scheduled commercial banks is 9%, which is higher than the 8% minimum prescribed under the Basel III international framework.
statement_analysis.reason: RBI has prescribed a minimum CRAR of 9% for Indian banks, reflecting a conservative regulatory stance that exceeds the Basel III minimum of 8%.

statement_analysis.statement: Statement 2: The additional Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) capital surcharge required of SBI as a Domestic Systemically Important Bank can be met by holding Tier 2 capital instruments such as subordinated debt, provided the overall CRAR requirement is satisfied.
statement_analysis.reason: The D-SIB CET1 surcharge must specifically be held in the form of Common Equity Tier 1 capital — Tier 2 instruments do not qualify for meeting this specific surcharge, regardless of overall CRAR satisfaction.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Students may mark both statements as correct by reasoning that 'if total CRAR is satisfied and Tier 2 is part of capital, it should logically count' — missing the regulatory specificity that the D-SIB surcharge is a CET1-only requirement.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: India's CRAR minimum is 9% vs. Basel III's 8% — this is a well-established fact. Statement 1 is correct.

Evaluate Statement 2: The D-SIB additional surcharge is mandated in the form of CET1 capital only. Tier 2 instruments (subordinated debt, redeemable preference shares) cannot substitute for this specific requirement. Statement 2 is incorrect.
Statement 1 correct, Statement 2 incorrect — option (c): 'Statement 1 is correct but Statement 2 is incorrect.'
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 uses a scope-extension logic trap: students know that overall CRAR can include Tier 1 and Tier 2 capital, and they extend this composability to the D-SIB surcharge. The trap works because 'satisfying CRAR through Tier 2' is a legitimate general banking concept — but the D-SIB framework specifically carves out the additional surcharge as a CET1-only buffer, reflecting regulators' desire for the highest-quality, loss-absorbing capital to backstop systemically important banks.
solution.final_explanation:
Capital adequacy norms for SBI operate at two levels — the general CRAR requirement and the additional D-SIB surcharge.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Basel III sets a minimum CRAR of 8% for internationally active banks. India's RBI has prescribed 9% as the minimum for all scheduled commercial banks — a 1 percentage point conservative buffer that reflects RBI's historically prudent approach to bank capital regulation.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The additional CET1 capital surcharge imposed on D-SIBs (0.60% for SBI in Bucket 4) must be maintained exclusively in the form of Common Equity Tier 1 capital — ordinary equity shares and retained earnings, essentially. Tier 2 instruments such as subordinated debt or hybrid capital do not qualify for this specific requirement, even if the bank's overall CRAR meets the minimum. The D-SIB surcharge represents the 'cleanest' form of loss-absorbing capital.

Value Addition:
• The Basel III capital framework has three tiers: CET1 (purest equity), Additional Tier 1 (AT1 bonds), and Tier 2 (subordinated debt).
• AT1 bonds (perpetual debt instruments) gained notoriety in India after the Yes Bank AT1 bond write-down in 2020.
• India's conservation buffer of 2.5% (also in CET1) is separate from the D-SIB surcharge.

solution.concept_anchor: Provisioning Coverage Ratio NPA health indicator
solution.strong_distractor: a — Net Interest Margin is a well-known banking profitability metric and students may select it as the indicator of NPA management health, not distinguishing between a profitability metric and an asset quality metric.
elimination_logic: Eliminate (a): Net Interest Margin (NIM) measures the difference between interest income earned and interest paid relative to assets — it is a profitability metric, not an NPA management indicator.
Eliminate (b): Return on Assets (RoA) measures overall profitability relative to total assets — again a profitability metric, not specific to NPA health.
Eliminate (d): Credit-Deposit Ratio measures how much of deposits are deployed as loans — it is a liquidity/efficiency metric, not an NPA management health indicator.

Confirm (c): Provisioning Coverage Ratio (PCR) measures the proportion of bad loans that a bank has already set aside provisions for — directly measuring the adequacy of a bank's buffer against NPA losses, making it the standard NPA health indicator.
solution.final_explanation:
Banks use various financial ratios to assess different aspects of performance; selecting the right ratio for the right dimension is a key analytical skill.

• Option (a) — Net Interest Margin (NIM): Incorrect. NIM = (Interest Income – Interest Expense) / Average Earning Assets. It measures interest profitability, not NPA management adequacy.
• Option (b) — Return on Assets (RoA): Incorrect. RoA = Net Profit / Total Assets. It measures overall asset efficiency/profitability, not the health of NPA management.
• Option (c) — Provisioning Coverage Ratio (PCR): Correct. PCR = Provisions held for NPAs / Gross NPAs. A higher PCR indicates that the bank has set aside proportionally more provisions against bad loans, signaling stronger NPA management and a better buffer against future credit losses. RBI has historically recommended a PCR of at least 70%.
• Option (d) — Credit-Deposit Ratio: Incorrect. This ratio shows what proportion of deposits are deployed as loans — a liquidity management and business model indicator, not an NPA health metric.

Value Addition:
• RBI had previously recommended a minimum PCR of 70% for banks; SBI's PCR trend is closely watched post-AQR.
• A declining PCR signals that provisions are not keeping pace with NPA growth — a red flag.
• Gross NPA ratio and Net NPA ratio (after provisioning) are often reported together with PCR for a complete picture.

solution.concept_anchor: SBI transformation chronology 1921 1955 2007 2017
solution.strong_distractor: c — Students who confuse the sequence of SBI's milestones, particularly placing the 2007 RBI divestment before the 1955 nationalization event, will select (c) — an error arising from treating 'divestment' as an earlier privatization step.
elimination_logic: Formation of Imperial Bank of India: 1921 — clearly the first event.
Constitution of SBI under SBI Act: 1955 — second, converting the Imperial Bank into SBI.
RBI divestment of majority stake to GoI: 2007 — third milestone in ownership history.
2017 mega-merger of associate banks and Bharatiya Mahila Bank: 2017 — most recent event. Correct order: 1921 → 1955 → 2007 → 2017 — option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The 2007 divestment is the trickiest sequencing element. Students who remember 'RBI owned SBI, then GoI took over' without attaching the year 2007 to this transition may place it incorrectly — either too early (thinking it happened soon after 1955) or too late (after 2017). The chronology trap is designed so that options (a) and (c) both involve plausible-sounding sequence inversions that test whether the student has a clear timeline.
solution.final_explanation:
SBI's institutional evolution spans nearly a century and involves four landmark events.

Correct sequence: Imperial Bank (1921) → SBI constituted (1955) → RBI divests stake to GoI (2007) → Associate bank mega-merger (2017) — option (b).

• 1921: Three colonial Presidency Banks merged to form the Imperial Bank of India, the largest commercial bank in British India.
• 1955: The State Bank of India Act transformed the Imperial Bank into SBI, a statutory corporation with RBI as majority shareholder — the starting point of India's public banking history.
• 2007: The SBI (Amendment) Act facilitated the transfer of RBI's majority shareholding to the Government of India, restructuring the ownership hierarchy without changing SBI's operational character.
• 2017: The merger of five associate banks and Bharatiya Mahila Bank into SBI created India's largest bank, crossing the ₹20 lakh crore balance sheet milestone.

Value Addition:
• The 1955 transformation was distinct from the 1969 bank nationalization: SBI was 'constituted,' not 'nationalized.'
• State Bank of Saurashtra merged with SBI in 2008 and State Bank of Indore in 2010 — both preceded the 2017 mega-merger.
• Each of these milestones had a distinct legislative vehicle: Imperial Bank Act → SBI Act 1955 → SBI Amendment Act 2007 → Companies Act/SBI Act provisions for 2017 merger.

SBI's Legal and Ownership Structure

solution.concept_anchor: SBI statutory corporation not Companies Act company legislative distinctiveness
solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who know that large government-owned enterprises are generally subject to Companies Act provisions may assume the same applies to SBI, not realizing that SBI's own special statute takes precedence.
elimination_logic: The scenario presents a bank established by a special parliamentary statute and asks which principle determines its legal standing and governance.

Eliminate (a): Companies Act applies to companies incorporated under it — SBI was constituted under its own special statute (SBI Act, 1955), making it a statutory corporation, not a Companies Act company.

Eliminate (b): The Banking Regulation Act, 1949 applies broadly to all banking companies and scheduled banks, but it does not exclusively determine SBI's governance structure — the SBI Act is the primary instrument.
Eliminate (d): RBI Act provisions govern RBI's regulatory functions over banks, not SBI's internal legal character as a corporation.

Confirm (c): The principle that a bank established by a special statute of Parliament is a 'statutory corporation' — distinct from a company — governs SBI's legal standing, determining its audit, governance, and regulatory treatment.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Option (a) traps students who apply the general rule 'government-owned companies are governed by Companies Act' to SBI. In reality, entities created directly by Parliamentary statute — like SBI, RBI, NABARD, LIC — are statutory corporations. The Companies Act only applies to entities incorporated under that Act. SBI's governance traces back to the SBI Act, 1955, not to company law. This distinction affects how SBI's accounts are audited, how directors are appointed, and whether its employees are 'government servants.'
solution.final_explanation:
A public sector financial institution was established through a dedicated Act of Parliament that defines its objectives, board composition, capital structure, and governance. The institution is not registered under the general company law. A legal question arises: what principle governs this institution's classification, audit accountability, and regulatory framework?

• Option (a) — Companies Act as primary governance framework: Incorrect. The Companies Act governs entities incorporated under it. An institution created by special statute is a 'statutory corporation' — a constitutionally distinct category.
• Option (b) — Banking Regulation Act exclusively: Incorrect. While the Banking Regulation Act applies to SBI's banking operations, it does not determine SBI's fundamental legal character as a corporation.
• Option (c) — Statutory corporation principle: Correct. The institution is a statutory corporation — it owes its existence to a special legislative act. This means its governance, audit (by CAG given government ownership), and appointment framework are determined by its own Act, not by the Companies Act. This precisely describes SBI.
• Option (d) — RBI Act provisions: Incorrect. RBI Act governs RBI's functions as central bank and regulator; it does not determine the corporate character of banks like SBI.

Value Addition:
• Other statutory corporations in finance: RBI (RBI Act, 1934), NABARD (NABARD Act, 1981), EXIM Bank, NHB — each has its own special statute.
• CAG audit of SBI flows from its government ownership threshold (substantial government investment), not from Companies Act provisions.
• Employees of statutory corporations are not necessarily civil servants; their service conditions are governed by institution-specific regulations.

solution.concept_anchor: NPA resolution mechanisms SARFAESI IBC DRT SAMG
solution.strong_distractor: b — The Stressed Assets Management Group (SAMG) is a real internal SBI mechanism, but students unfamiliar with SBI's internal organizational structure may consider it a fabrication and eliminate it as the odd one out, while the actual odd item is the Debt Restructuring Oversight Committee, which belongs to a different framework.
elimination_logic: The question asks for the mechanism that does NOT belong among the recognized formal legal or institutional frameworks for NPA resolution used by SBI.
SARFAESI Act: Real and widely used legal mechanism for secured asset recovery — belongs.
Stressed Assets Management Group (SAMG): Real internal SBI unit for managing stressed accounts — belongs.
Joint Lenders' Forum (JLF): Real inter-creditor coordination mechanism introduced by RBI for large stressed accounts — belongs.

Strategic Debt Restructuring (SDR) Oversight Authority: This is a fabricated institutional name; SDR is a real scheme but there is no separate 'SDR Oversight Authority' as a formal institution — this is the odd one out → option (d).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Option (d) deploys plausible-fabrication: 'Strategic Debt Restructuring (SDR) Oversight Authority' sounds like a real regulatory body because SDR is a genuine RBI scheme (allowing banks to convert debt to equity and change management in defaulting companies). Students who are aware of the SDR scheme but not of the institutional architecture around it may assume an 'Oversight Authority' exists, making them hesitate to eliminate it. The key distinction is that SDR is a scheme/mechanism, not an institutional body with a separate oversight authority.
solution.final_explanation:
SBI employs multiple institutional mechanisms for NPA resolution, both legal and administrative.

• Option (a) — SARFAESI Act: A real and extensively used mechanism. The Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interests Act, 2002 allows SBI to enforce security interests and recover dues without court proceedings.
• Option (b) — Stressed Assets Management Group (SAMG): A real internal SBI organizational unit dedicated to monitoring and resolving large stressed accounts, coordinating with other lenders and resolution professionals.
• Option (c) — Joint Lenders' Forum (JLF): A real RBI-mandated inter-creditor coordination mechanism introduced in 2014 for accounts with aggregate exposure above a threshold; SBI often serves as lead bank in JLFs.
• Option (d) — Strategic Debt Restructuring (SDR) Oversight Authority: This is the odd one out. SDR is a real RBI scheme (2015) that enables a consortium of lenders to convert outstanding debt to equity and acquire majority stake in a defaulting company. However, there is no separate formal body called the 'SDR Oversight Authority' — the scheme is administered through the existing JLF and lender consortium mechanisms.

Value Addition:
• The SDR scheme was introduced by RBI in June 2015 to address the problem of promoter-led defaults.
• IBC 2016 largely superseded JLF and SDR mechanisms for large corporate insolvencies.
• SBI's total NPA exposure, concentrated in infrastructure, power, and steel sectors, remains a key financial sector risk indicator.

solution.concept_anchor: SLR G-Sec SBI Primary Dealer PDMA reform implications

statement_analysis.statement: The Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR) obligates banks including SBI to maintain a specified proportion of their Net Demand and Time Liabilities (NDTL) in the form of approved securities, which primarily consist of Government Securities and State Development Loans.
statement_analysis.reason: SLR is maintained in approved securities (G-Secs, SDLs, and certain other approved instruments) as a specified percentage of NDTL — this is an accurate description.

statement_analysis.statement: Since SBI holds Primary Dealer (PD) status, it is the sole underwriter of all Government Securities issued in India, and no other institution can participate in primary auctions of G-Secs.
statement_analysis.reason: There are multiple Primary Dealers (both bank-PDs and standalone PDs) authorized to participate in G-Sec primary auctions. SBI is one among several PDs, not the exclusive underwriter.

statement_analysis.statement: The proposed establishment of a Public Debt Management Agency (PDMA) as an independent body could potentially alter SBI's current role as a Primary Dealer, as debt management functions would be consolidated under a separate institutional framework.
statement_analysis.reason: The PDMA proposal aims to separate sovereign debt management from the central bank; this restructuring could affect the existing PD framework and the roles of bank-PDs like SBI in government securities operations.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Students who accept Statement 2's 'sole underwriter' claim without scrutiny (because SBI is indeed the largest single buyer of G-Secs) will mark all three as correct and choose (d).
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: SLR in approved securities (G-Secs, SDLs) as a percentage of NDTL — accurately described. Statement 1 correct.
Evaluate Statement 2: Multiple Primary Dealers exist in India (SBI, HDFC Bank, ICICI Bank, standalone PDs like PNB Gilts, I-Sec PD, etc.); SBI is not the sole underwriter — Statement 2 is incorrect.
Evaluate Statement 3: PDMA reform could restructure the PD framework — this is a recognized reform debate. Statement 3 correct.
Statements 1 and 3 correct — option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 uses a scope-extension trap: SBI is the largest institutional holder of G-Secs and has PD status, which leads many students to assume it holds exclusive underwriting authority. In reality, India's PD system is designed for market-making across multiple institutions — both bank-PDs (SBI, HDFC Bank, ICICI Bank, Axis Bank, etc.) and standalone PDs — to ensure competitive price discovery and prevent concentration of sovereign debt underwriting.
solution.final_explanation:
India's Government Securities market and SBI's role in it involve several distinct mechanisms.

• Statement 1 — Correct: SLR requires banks to maintain approved securities (primarily G-Secs and SDLs) equivalent to a percentage of their NDTL. RBI periodically revises the SLR; SBI's large balance sheet makes it one of the largest G-Sec holders in India.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: India has a network of authorized Primary Dealers — both 'Bank-PDs' (commercial banks authorized as PDs) and 'Standalone PDs' (dedicated non-bank entities). SBI is one of multiple PDs; it is not the sole underwriter. Each PD has minimum underwriting commitment obligations at auctions.
• Statement 3 — Correct: The PDMA proposal would create an independent agency to manage sovereign debt, potentially reducing RBI's direct role and restructuring the PD framework. This is an ongoing reform debate with implications for SBI's PD activities.

solution.strong_distractor: b — The pairing of 'RBI Governor — appointed by the Prime Minister' sounds authoritative since the PM heads the Union Government and signs off on important appointments, but the formal appointment is made by the Cabinet (Government of India) on PM's recommendation — and more critically, SBI's Chairman appointment (not RBI Governor) requires RBI consultation.
elimination_logic: Evaluate (a): SBI Chairman is appointed by the Government of India in consultation with RBI — this is correct per the SBI Act, 1955. Pairing is accurate.

Evaluate (b): The RBI Governor is appointed by the Government of India (specifically, the Cabinet Committee on Appointments), not exclusively by the Prime Minister — additionally, FSIB recommends SBI positions, not RBI Governor appointment.

Evaluate (d): The Finance Minister directly approves SBI Chairman appointment is not entirely accurate as a standalone fact — it goes through the FSIB recommendation process and formal GoI appointment in consultation with RBI.

solution.final_explanation:
The appointment process for top positions at India's major financial institutions has distinct pathways that are frequently tested.

• Option (b) — RBI Governor: appointed by the Prime Minister after recommendation by FSIB: Incorrect. The RBI Governor is appointed by the Government of India (Cabinet); the FSIB does not recommend RBI Governor appointments — FSIB's mandate covers PSBs and financial institutions, not the RBI itself.
